title: Dense correspondence and interpretable skeletal morphospaces
introduction: Comparative skeletal biology seeks to relate anatomical variation to function and evolutionary history. The primate cuboid, a bone of the lateral midfoot, presents a demanding case: its joint surfaces, plantar tuberosity and peroneus longus tendon groove form a complex anatomy relevant to foot mechanics. [@bojsen1979] [@nowak2010] Comparing this anatomy requires measuring differences across curved surfaces, articular margins and local relief, not only at isolated points.

sections.heading: The methodological gap
paragraphs: Three-dimensional scans capture detailed surfaces, but do not establish which locations correspond between specimens. Anatomical landmarks provide expert-defined anchors, yet may undersample variation between them. [@watanabe2018] Earlier work, including morphVQ, brought learned descriptors and functional maps into biological morphometrics. [@thomas2023] This study connects anatomically constrained dense matching to a reconstruction-capable morphospace, so that statistical variation can be examined as changes in surface anatomy.

sections.heading: A two-stage approach
paragraphs: Stage 1 builds dense correspondences across a sparse network of specimens and templates. The functional-map formulation and Panine et al.'s landmark-adapted bases provide the initial matching framework. [@ovsjanikov2012] [@panine2022] Anatomical anchors, surface diagnostics and targeted refinement address discontinuities, collapse and incomplete coverage. The revised mandible models shown here instead use separately initialized maps based on Surface Maps via Adaptive Triangulations, with project-specific safeguards. [@schmidt2023] Correspondence is a methodological component in its own right because matching errors propagate into shape analysis.

Stage 2 uses functional-map networks and a limit-shape common basis to make surface features comparable across specimens. [@huang2014] [@huang2019] The autoencoder builds on DISCO-AE, with DiffusionNet surface layers and an SNK-inspired prism decoder adapted for reconstruction from a common latent code. [@hahner2024] [@sharp2022] [@attaiki2023] Principal-component analysis (PCA) summarizes variation in those codes. Decoding along the axes reveals associated anatomical changes, linking statistical relationships among specimens to surface geometry.

sections.heading: Study scope and initial results
paragraphs: Anthropoid cuboids are the primary application. A non-fossil hominoid subset examines the same element within a narrower taxonomic range; mouse mandibles and humeri test the approach on different skeletal geometries. The current models produce reconstructed surfaces and decoded shape variation for all four datasets. These outputs make local contours, projections and depressions available for anatomical inspection alongside specimen relationships in the morphospace.

Earlier development analyses found agreement between learned shape relationships and manual-landmark and automated pseudolandmark morphometrics, with decoded cuboid axes localizing articular and plantar variation. These findings concern earlier model versions. Reconstruction, morphometric agreement, repeatability, phylogenetic signal and size associations are being reassessed for the revised datasets and models shown here.

sections.heading: Biological significance
paragraphs: The contribution is a connection between whole-surface measurement and anatomical explanation, complementing established geometric morphometrics. Instead of stopping at separation in a scatterplot, researchers can examine where and how surfaces differ and formulate explicit hypotheses about joint form, tendon pathways and skeletal diversity. Such hypotheses still require comparative or biomechanical tests: decoded variation alone does not establish locomotor adaptation or evolutionary causation.
